See every workspace, open a live terminal, type into it, and get notified when a coding agent needs you. You don't need to sign in to cmux. Everything runs between your phone and your own computer, over a private network you control, with no cloud service in the middle. Tailscale is the easiest way to set that up. Another VPN, a trusted local network, or a Cloudflare Tunnel behind Cloudflare Access also work. Important This is an independent project. It is not made, endorsed, or supported by Manaflow or the cmux team. Features Answer agent permission requests, questions and plans from a notification or a home screen widget. See Claude Code, Codex and Pi sessions as a chat, and reply with text, voice, @ file mentions and photos. Start a new agent task in a folder or open workspace, or resume a past session. Get every cmux notification on your phone, with inline replies, bubbles and background delivery. Organize workspaces: create, rename, pin, recolor, group, and track agent status and unread counts. Use a live terminal with sticky modifier keys, local scrollback and copy. Share text and links from any app to an agent. Check each computer's CPU and RAM, keep it awake, and manage cmux Cloud VMs and automations. Open a terminal's ports in your phone's browser over Tailscale. Lock the app with your fingerprint, face or screen lock. How it works muxer is a small program that runs on your computer. It talks to cmux through cmux's local control socket, forwards only the commands the app needs, and streams a terminal to the phone as changed rows only. The phone reaches the relay through an HTTPS proxy in front of it that only your devices can reach, such as tailscale serve . See Reaching the relay for the options. Set up your computer You need cmux 0.65 or later on the computer, and a way for the phone to reach the computer over HTTPS. The steps below use Tailscale, signed in on the computer and on the phone. For other setups, see Reaching the relay . Install the relay with Homebrew : brew install gantoine/tap/muxer Other ways to install it Download muxer-<version>-darwin-arm64.tar.gz (Apple silicon) or -darwin-amd64.tar.gz (Intel) from the releases page , check it against SHA256SUMS , extract it, and move muxer into a folder on your PATH . The binary is not notarized by Apple. If you downloaded it with a browser, run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine muxer before the first run. Let the relay talk to cmux. By default cmux only accepts programs started inside cmux terminals. The relay runs in the background, so switch the socket mode to password (recommended) or automation : In cmux, open Settings › Automation and set socket access to Password , then set a password. The relay reads it from ~/.local/state/cmux/socket-control-password , the same file the cmux CLI uses. Or set "automation": { "socketControlMode": "automation" } in ~/.config/cmux/cmux.json . This lets any program running as your user control cmux without a password. Start the relay at login. muxer install Make it reachable from your phone only. With Tailscale: tailscale serve --bg --https=8765 http://127.0.0.1:8765 Check everything. muxer doctor Pair your phone Install the APK from the releases page . To check it first, run apksigner verify --print-certs muxer-<version>.apk and compare the SHA-256 certificate fingerprint with this one: 9D:6C:85:65:17:81:34:51:CF:1D:82:8F:BC:A0:AE:91:B0:D4:C5:92:B0:74:04:0F:72:19:19:DB:C5:61:5C:8B Then run this on your computer: muxer pair muxer pair uses the computer's Tailscale name. If the phone reaches the relay another way, pass that address: muxer pair --url https://muxer.example.com . Scan the QR code with your phone's camera, or tap Pair a computer in the app and type the address and code. The code works once and expires after 10 minutes. Each paired computer shows up in the app's Computers list. Reaching the relay The app only talks to the relay over HTTPS and only accepts certificates from a public certificate authority, so plain HTTP and self-signed certificates do not work. Keep the relay on 127.0.0.1 and put something in front of it that adds HTTPS and lets only your own devices through: Tailscale: tailscale serve does both. It adds a certificate for the computer's tailnet name and keeps the relay inside your tailnet. muxer pair and muxer doctor set it up for you. Another VPN (WireGuard, ZeroTier and so on) or your local network: run a reverse proxy such as Caddy on the computer. Point a domain you own at the computer's private address and get a Let's Encrypt certificate with a DNS challenge. Only do this on a network where you trust every device. Cloudflare Tunnel: put the relay behind Cloudflare Access so only your devices get through. The app cannot complete a browser sign-in, so Access has to recognize the phone another way, for example through the Cloudflare One (WARP) client enrolled in your Zero Trust organization. Then pair with that address using muxer pair --url . Opening a terminal's ports When your phone reaches the computer through Tailscale, a terminal's menu has Open ports in Tailscale . It lists the ports that terminal's programs listen on. Tap a port to open it in your phone's browser at the computer's Tailscale name, for example http://my-mac.tailnet.ts.net:3000 . The phone connects to it directly over your tailnet, not through the relay. A server that only listens on 127.0.0.1 can't be reached that way, so its port has a switch. Turning it on exposes the port with tailscale serve , which gives it an https:// address on the same port. Every device on your tailnet can then reach it , not just your phone. Turn the switch off to stop exposing it. The computer's settings in the app list every port Muxer exposed, including ones whose terminal has closed. This only works with Tailscale for now. Custom alerts with cmux automations The phone shows every notification cmux posts, so a cmux automation with a notify action also reaches your phone. For example, this rule in ~/.cmuxterm/automations.json tells you when cmux types "continue" for an agent after an overload: { "version" : 1 , "rules" : [ { "id" : " phone-auto-resume " , "when" : { "event" : " agent.auto_resume.sent " }, "then" : [ { "action" : " notify " , "title" : " Agent resumed " , "body" : " {{payload.agent}} was resumed after a temporary error (attempt {{payload.attempt}}). " } ] } ] } Run cmux automation reload after editing the file, and cmux automation test phone-auto-resume --event '{"name":"agent.auto_resume.sent","category":"agent","payload":{"agent":"claude","attempt":1}}' to check a rule without firing it. On the phone, open a computer's settings and tap Automations to see its rules. You can turn each one on or off, see what it reacts to and what it does, read its recent activity, and reload the file after you edit it. Writing new rules still happens in the file on the computer. Updating the relay brew upgrade muxer muxer install Running muxer install again restarts the background relay on the new version. Managing phones muxer devices # list paired phones muxer revoke DEVICE_ID # disconnect a phone and make it pair again muxer uninstall # stop the relay and remove it from login items Security The phone can do what you can do in cmux: read every terminal and type into it. Pair only phones you control, and revoke lost ones. Each phone gets its own random token. The computer stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, in ~/Library/Application Support/muxer/devices.json (mode 0600). The phone keeps it encrypted with a key in the Android Keystore. Turn on Lock Muxer in the app's settings to ask for your fingerprint, face or screen lock when the app opens or comes back after a minute away (you can pick a longer time). Notifications then show only a generic line on the lock screen if the phone is set to hide sensitive notification content there (Settings › Notifications › Notifications on lock screen), answers and replies from notifications need an unlocked phone, widgets show only counts, and the app stays out of the recents screen. Pairing codes are single-use, expire after 10 minutes, and stop working after 10 wrong guesses. The relay listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Put it behind an HTTPS proxy that only your devices can reach, such as tailscale serve . Never expose it with tailscale funnel , an open port, or a tunnel without access control. Opening a port that listens only on 127.0.0.1 runs tailscale serve for it, which makes it reachable from every device on your tailnet until you stop exposing it. The relay only does this for ports your cmux terminals listen on, never for its own port, and never uses tailscale funnel . It only removes serve entries it created. Pairing, listing, and revoking go through a Unix socket that only your user can open, so none of them can be done over the network. The relay only forwards the commands listed in the relay protocol . It is not a general cmux socket proxy. Development See DEVELOPMENT.md for building, testing, releasing, and the relay protocol. License MIT. See LICENSE . The logo remixes the chevron from the cmux icon. cmux and its logo belong to Manaflow, Inc. Using them here does not mean Manaflow made, endorses, or supports this project. If you are from Manaflow and want the logo changed, open an issue. post.title: Check your cmux sessions from Android
post.promise: Muxer links an Android app to cmux terminals through a relay on your computer.
post.whatItIs: Muxer is an open source relay and Android app for viewing and controlling cmux terminal sessions over a private network. A beginner could test a narrow setup guide or onboarding aid as a separate project; that adaptation is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who use cmux and want to check sessions from a phone might pay for setup help or a simpler companion. The source gives no customer or payment evidence.
loop: Install the relay on a Mac with cmux.
Put the relay behind HTTPS access limited to your own devices.
Pair the Android app using a one-time code.
Review sessions and notifications on the phone.
Revoke a paired device if it is lost.
post.evidence: The project README describes the relay, Android app, pairing flow, terminal controls, and private-network setup.
post.uncertainty: This is a documented product description, not independent evidence of customer use. Access setup requires care: the phone can read terminals and type into cmux. A human must manage network exposure and decide which devices to pair.
first24Hours: Read the README security and setup sections.
Write down the steps needed for a private HTTPS setup.
Ask one cmux user to review a hypothetical beginner setup guide.

ease.reason: The README gives concrete setup steps, but a first test needs cmux, Android, and private HTTPS networking.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: cmux users wanting phone access might pay for setup help; the source establishes no buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A narrow setup guide is plausible in four weeks; validating the workflow requires access to cmux and Android.

autonomy.reason: Relay streaming and notifications repeat automatically, while device pairing and network access need human oversight.

evidence.reason: The README documents a working relay and app workflow, but offers no cited evidence of real use.

sources.text: AI Workflow Automation Platform - n8n n8n.io Product Use cases Docs Community Enterprise Pricing Sign in Get started Product Use cases Docs Community Enterprise Pricing See llms.txt for all machine-readable content. Agent, workflow, or both? Agent, workflow, or both? The less of the process you can define, the more agent you need. You pick the point on the dial. Start building Talk to sales Deterministic AI Agent Autonomous 1 2 3 Change Deterministic workflows For when nothing about your workflow is unknown in advance. </> You define every step Nothing is decided at runtime </> No memory needed The same input gives the same result </> Runs on a trigger A schedule, a webhook, an event </> No model calls So no token spend at all Nightly report Order sync Lead routing case Deterministic Agentic Autonomous Why build ai agents in n8n? You can’t control agents that you can’t understand Agents you can audit, always Test how your agents behave before you hit publish. Open any step to see the inputs and outputs. Open up any session, any tool call. Replay any run to find where it broke. The predictable path to prod Publish in one click. Scheduling, error-handling, versioning, and execution logs come built in. Set the tools an agent can reach and actions that need a human. Self-host to keep data in-house. Every integration is a tool Give agents 600+ native integrations and your own workflows as tools. No need to rebuild APIs from scratch. One company. One workspace. Different team, different AI tool. And nobody knows what exists. In n8n, agents and workflows live in one workspace your teams can see and reuse — with access control on the ones that matter. Your token spend, tamed Not every action needs an agent. So n8n doesn’t force you to use one. Mix deterministic logic with judgment only where it earns it — and stop burning AI budget on everything else. One platform for all your agents and workflows Workflows are your deterministic backbone. Agents add judgment and continuity on top. In n8n, they call each other in the same UI. Start building Play video Turn plain text into production-ready agents Describe it to the AI Assistant. Prompt it via the MCP server. Or build it by hand. n8n drafts the setup — then you test and publish. Start building But can’t I just build in a coding agent? If it’s just you, use Claude Code or Codex. Once work touches company systems and outlives whoever built it, a conversation isn’t enough. Who depends on it? Coding agents n8n Just you (you watch it run) The fastest way to get it done Overkill for a one-off task Just you (runs while you sleep) If you wire up the scheduling, retries, and alerts yourself All come built-in to the platform Your team The record lives on your machine A shared run history anyone can open and understand Your customers Whoever runs it sets the limits Tool limits and approval steps set before anyone runs it Ai agent template library Where there’s a will, there’s already a workflow 9,000+ community-built templates make getting started with agentic workflows simple. Even if you’re new to agents. Sticky Note AI Agent Simple Memory +2 Build your first AI agent Lucas Peyrin RAG chatbot for company documents using Google Drive and Gemini Google Drive Google Drive Trigger Sticky Note +9 AI chatbot that can search the web Sticky Note AI Agent OpenAI Chat Model +4 Autonomous AI crawler HTTP Request Merge Edit Fields (Set) +13 Chat with a Google Sheet using AI Google Sheets Edit Fields (Set) Switch +8 AI agent that can scrape webpages HTTP Request If Edit Fields (Set) +7 Personal life manager with Telegram, Google services & voice-enabled AI If Edit Fields (Set) Telegram +6 Explore templates Reliable agents, ready for enterprise Explore enterprise Get started Security + control Fully on-prem option, SSO SAML, and LDAP, encrypted secret stores, version control, RBAC permissions. Observability + transparency Audit logs and log streaming to your SIEM, workflow history, real-time alerts, usage dashboards. Developer experience Git-based control, isolated environments, multi-user workflows, workflow diffs. AI governance Human-in-the-loop, guardrails, evaluations. FAQs What’s the difference between the AI Agent node and the autonomous AI agent? The AI Agent node is one step inside of a workflow that runs to completion. An autonomous agent is a standalone entity that exists between runs. With AI Agent nodes, you connect them to an AI model, memory, and tools so that it can execute a judgment call within a defined process. When you can list all the steps of the flow you want to build before you start, the AI Agent node is what you build. Autonomous agents use models to decide how to act, have their own addressable identity, and persistent memory. These agents are the right choice for long, complex, judgment-heavy processes that don’t follow a set path each time. Can I still use the AI Agent node in workflows? Absolutely. The AI Agent node — and workflows in general — aren’t going anywhere. Deterministic, auditable execution still matters as much as it did, and every workflow you’ve already built becomes a tool your autonomous agents can use. Existing users actually start ahead. Can workflows and agents work together? Yes. Workflows become tools an agent calls. Workflows can call published agents with the ‘Message an Agent’ node. How do I build an autonomous agent? Use the AI Assistant to describe the agent you want to build in natural language (recommended) or build it manually in the Agent Builder. Can I test my autonomous agent before I publish? Yes, you can do a test run of your agent’s behavior before it goes live to see if it works as you intended. What can a standalone agent remember? Session memory by default. Cross-session (episodic) memory is opt-in and needs an OpenAI credential. How are standalone agents priced? One turn with an agent is one execution. Sub-agent and workflow-tool calls don’t add extra. Agents share the same execution quota as workflows. Can external systems call my autonomous agents? Not at the moment. The ability to call n8n agents from external agents and MCP servers is on the roadmap. Watch this space. Start with a prompt. Ship something that lasts. A sealed letter for your quick questions on macOS. Write on the parchment, a quill writes the answer back, and the letter burns when you're done. Website · English · 简体中文 The letter Press ⌥H anywhere. A letter settles at the top of the screen, already sealed in wax. Parchment, not a text box. The paper has deckled edges, fibers and a fold crease. Your question sits on a ruled line, and the answer is set in a book face below it. The sheet grows with the answer up to an A4 page, then follows the quill. A quill that writes. Answers stream in at a hand's pace. Fresh ink glows gold before it settles to sepia, and the quill rests after the last word. While the model thinks, the quill hovers and counts the seconds. Wax seals. The crimson seal names the model writing to you. Paste a long text or a picture, or capture a region of the screen, and it is sealed into an amber seal cut with runes instead of filling your question. Burn after reading. Press Esc or click outside, and the letter catches fire at its bottom edge. Scorch, embers and sparks climb to the seal, and the conversation goes with them. Nothing is saved. Esc, and it burns Candlelit paper in Dark Mode Reduce Motion turns off the falling paper, the stamping, the ink shimmer and the fire. The text simply appears. Install Download Howler.dmg , open it, and drag Howler onto Applications. Older versions and Howler.zip (the same app) are on Releases . Open Howler. It is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it opens like any other app. Updates keep your Keychain and screen-recording permissions. A small quill appears in the menu bar. Howler has no Dock icon. From v0.1.7 on, Howler updates itself. Choose Check for Updates… in the menu, or let it check once a day (Settings › General). A new version shows up quietly in the menu and in Settings instead of popping up a window. Nothing installs until you say so. Updates are installed by Sparkle , which checks the download's EdDSA signature and Developer ID first. Versions up to 0.1.6 need one manual download. Releases before v0.1.4 were ad-hoc signed. If Gatekeeper stops one of those, right-click it and choose Open . Set up a model Howler writes with one model service. The setup is short enough to hand to an AI assistant. Open Settings › General › Copy Setup Prompt and paste it into Claude Code, Codex or another assistant that can run commands. It asks which service and model you want, checks the official docs, writes the setup and runs a check until it passes. It never asks for your API key in the chat. When it needs the key, it asks you to copy it, then runs pbpaste | Howler config set api-key --stdin , which sends the key straight into the Keychain. You can run the same commands yourself. They live in the app binary: H=/Applications/Howler.app/Contents/MacOS/Howler $H config schema # every field, with examples $H config set preset=deepseek ' body={"thinking":{"type":"disabled"}} ' pbpaste | $H config set api-key --stdin # or --env NAME, --file PATH $H check # --verbose shows the request, key masked $H config show Field Meaning format chat-completions (OpenAI and compatible, including local Ollama / LM Studio), anthropic-messages , gemini-generate-content base-url API base without the endpoint path; https:// only, except http://localhost model Model name as the service spells it body JSON merged into every request, e.g. to turn thinking off or cap the output headers Extra HTTP headers. Never the key. preset openai , anthropic , gemini , xai , deepseek or openrouter . Fills the three fields above. Changes take effect in the running app at once. Every request goes straight to the service you configured, never through a relay. System prompt Every conversation starts with a short system prompt, shown in full in Settings › Prompt : The date, in UTC , e.g. Current date: 2026-10-29 (UTC). Without it a model takes its training cutoff for today. UTC says nothing about your time zone or location. Howler adds it; it can't be edited. Instructions , editable. The suggested ones ask for short answers without tables (the letter can't show them), in the language of your question. Reset brings them back. Leave the instructions empty to turn the whole prompt off, date included, for models that reject a system prompt. A body that sets system (Anthropic) or systemInstruction / system_instruction (Gemini) replaces it. The model can't search the web: it answers from what it was trained on, and the date only lets it say when something may be too recent for it. Use ⌥H Open the letter. Press again to burn it. The shortcut can be changed in Settings. ⌥, Open Settings from any app ↩ / ⌥↩ Send / new line ⌘C Copy the latest answer (or click ❧ Copy). With text selected, it copies the selection. + Attach Paste from the clipboard, or capture a screen region ⌘V Short text goes into the question. Text of 280+ characters or 3+ lines, or a picture, is sealed as an attachment, including an image copied in a browser or an image file copied in Finder. Esc / click outside Burn the letter, and the conversation with it Follow-up questions stay on the same sheet, separated by a fleuron. ⏹ stops a reply and keeps what is already written. Attachments travel only with your next question, so leave out passwords and other secrets. Screen capture asks for Screen & System Audio Recording permission the first time. Howler only takes a still image of the region you drag and never records audio; macOS simply grants screen and audio access together. Privacy No chat history, ever. Messages live in memory and burn with the letter. Stored: the model setup, its last check, your system prompt instructions and your shortcut (UserDefaults), plus the API key (Keychain). The system prompt carries the date in UTC and nothing about you: no name, language setting, time zone or location. The clipboard and the screen are read only when you paste or capture. No logs, no telemetry. Network requests use an ephemeral URLSession . Update checks fetch appcast.xml from Howler's latest GitHub Release, at most once a day, and only after you allow it. They send no system profile; GitHub sees only the request, with the app and Sparkle versions in its User-Agent. Turn them off in Settings › General. The command line never prints the key. Send Feedback… (in the menu, or in Settings › General) opens a GitHub issue form in your browser with Howler's version, the macOS version and the chip filled in. Nothing is sent until you submit it there. Build from source Requires Xcode 15.3+ (Swift 5.10+) and macOS 14+. The one third-party dependency is Sparkle (pinned in Package.swift ), which installs updates. make test # unit tests: config, requests, streaming, attachments, hotkeys, quill pacing make app # universal build → build/Howler.zip, app staged in build/stage.noindex (ad-hoc, or SIGN_IDENTITY) make dmg # the same app in build/Howler.dmg, beside an Applications link make run # build and open make icon # re-render Resources/AppIcon.icns from Sources/Howler/AppIconArt.swift Debug builds include a demo mode that needs no key and no network: swift build HOWLER_DEMO=1 .build/debug/Howler # also: long, multi, burn, image, setup, settings HOWLER_DEMO_DARK=1 HOWLER_DEMO=1 .build/debug/Howler To rename the app or change its bundle ID, edit app.config and rebuild. To release, bump VERSION there and push a matching v tag. CI tests, builds, signs, notarizes and publishes the release (see release signing ). Manual checks are listed in ACCEPTANCE.md . Upgrading from Napkin or QuickAsk The project was renamed QuickAsk → Napkin → Howler, and so was the GitHub repo. Update old clones with git remote set-url origin git@github.com:HiAriesZhou/Howler.git . The bundle ID com.hiarieszhou.howler shares nothing with com.hiarieszhou.napkin or io.github.hiarieszhou.quickask , so set up the model again. Delete the old app, because both would compete for ⌥Space. You can remove the old Keychain items in Keychain Access by searching for the old bundle IDs. The icon and seals are drawn in code with the letter's own paper, wax and fire. Provider marks are monochrome letters and SF Symbols; no trademarked logos are bundled. post.title: Ask a quick question, then clear the chat
post.promise: Howler puts a model-powered question and answer in a temporary macOS window.
post.whatItIs: Howler is a macOS menu bar app that sends questions to a model service the user configures, streams answers, and clears the conversation when closed. A beginner might explore a separate ephemeral note-taking tool; that adaptation is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: Mac users who want transient AI answers might pay for a privacy-focused utility. The attached README does not establish customer demand or sales.
loop: Configure a model service and store its API key in Keychain.
Open the letter and type a question.
Optionally attach pasted text, an image, or a screen capture.
Review the streamed answer and ask a follow-up.
Close the letter to clear the conversation from memory.
post.evidence: The README describes the menu bar interface, model configuration, streaming replies, attachments, and that messages live in memory and burn when the letter is closed.
post.uncertainty: The privacy and product details come from the project's own README, without independent validation. A person must configure a model, protect API credentials, and judge answer accuracy; attached content goes to the configured service.
first24Hours: Read the README's setup and privacy sections.
Try the documented demo mode without a key or network.
List what remains stored and what is sent to the configured model.

ease.reason: The README offers a demo mode without a key or network, while normal use requires macOS and model setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: some Mac users may pay for transient AI answers; the README provides no evidence of buyers or revenue.

feasibility.reason: A narrow demo is accessible, but building a comparable macOS app involves Swift and model-service setup.

autonomy.reason: Answer streaming and conversation clearing are automatic, but users configure services and review answers themselves.

evidence.reason: The first-party README documents a detailed product workflow and demo mode, without independent real-use evidence.

post.title: Howler: quick AI questions that disappear
post.promise: Try a macOS menu-bar chat that keeps conversation in memory and burns it when closed.
post.whatItIs: Howler is a macOS menu-bar app for quick AI questions. Its README says conversation text stays in memory and is removed when the letter is closed; requests go to a model service configured by the user.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a Mac user wanting transient AI chats might pay for this kind of app; the source provides no buyer or pricing evidence.
loop: Install Howler on a supported Mac.
Configure a model service and API key using the app setup.
Open a letter and enter a non-sensitive question.
Review the streamed answer and decide whether to follow it.
Close the letter to burn the conversation.
post.evidence: The GitHub README documents the macOS app, model configuration, streamed answers, and in-memory conversation behavior.
post.uncertainty: Project documentation does not establish independent use. Model setup requires a provider and credential. Closing removes conversation text according to the README, but setup and API key remain stored. People should avoid secrets and review answers; the app does not search the web.
first24Hours: Read the README privacy and setup sections.
Try demo mode or configure a model with a non-sensitive question.
Close the letter and confirm its conversation is gone; this would show whether the documented short-chat flow works.

ease.reason: README has setup instructions and demo mode, but model use requires macOS and configuration.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac users may value transient chats; the source gives no buyer, demand, or pricing evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test of a basic question-and-close flow is plausible, though provider setup is an obstacle.

autonomy.reason: Answers stream automatically, but people configure the provider, review responses, and close the chat.

evidence.reason: README documents app behavior and a no-key demo mode, without independent real-use evidence.
